screens.title: The for Loop: Iterating Over Sequences
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll meet the for loop, the Python construct for visiting each element in a sequence. You'll learn why iteration is a core programming pattern, how range generates number sequences, and how helpers like enumerate and zip make indexed and parallel loops simple. We will also compare for to while so you know when each is better, and explore control tools such as break, continue, and the less obvious for-else. Practical examples include iterating through a string to inspect characters, using range to count, enumerating a list to obtain indexes and values together, and zipping two lists to step through related data in parallel. By the end you will be confident choosing a for loop when the number of steps is known or when processing every element in a collection is the goal. A short coding activity will help you apply these ideas: printing even numbers, a multiplication table, counting vowels, and drawing a triangle with asterisks. Notice how iteration moves work from manual counters to clear, less error-prone code. Ready to explore how a small loop can repeatedly do useful work? Let's begin.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: A for loop visits each item in a sequence and runs the loop body for each item, making repetitive tasks concise and less error-prone.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Introduction
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

For loop essentials

Visit each element in a sequence and perform the same steps. Practical for strings, lists, and numeric sequences.

In this lesson
Understand how for walks sequences and why range uses a half-open interval.
Use enumerate and zip to access indexes or pair sequences cleanly.
Control flow inside loops with break and continue; learn the for-else pattern.
Why it matters

Loops let you transform or inspect many items with a few lines. They reduce bugs compared with manual counters and simplify data processing tasks.

Visual concept
Sequence
String, list, range
Loop Body
Code runs per item
Helpers
range, enumerate, zip
Explore key topics
range()
Generates integer sequences; stop value excluded.
enumerate()
Returns index and value together for indexed loops.
for-else
Else runs only if loop finishes without break.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Practice & Tools
Practice tasks
  • Print even numbers from 2 to 20 using range with a step of 2.

Toolbox reminders

screens.title: What a for Loop Is
screens.narratorSegment: A for loop is a control structure that visits each element in a sequence and executes the loop body for that element. Think of iteration as walking along a list of items and performing the same action at each step. The loop variable takes on each value in the sequence in order, so you do not need to manage a manual counter unless you explicitly want an index. A concrete example is iterating over the string 'Python' where the loop variable becomes 'P', then 'y', and so on, and the print function outputs each character. A helpful analogy is a conveyor belt: items come past a single processing station and are transformed or inspected one at a time. This contrasts with a while loop, which keeps running as long as a condition is true and is better when you cannot predict the number of iterations up front. A common misconception is thinking for loops only work with numbers; in reality any iterable sequence — strings, lists, ranges — works. Key takeaway: use for when you have a collection to step through. A quick self-check: can you explain why a manual index is unnecessary when the sequence provides each element?

keyIdea.title: Definition

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What a for Loop Is
Definition

A for loop visits every element of a sequence and runs the loop body once per element. The loop variable is assigned each element in turn, so you usually don't need an index.

Analogy: conveyor belt delivering items to a processing station, each item is handled once.
Concrete example: iterate characters in a string to count or transform them.
Common mistake: expecting for to include the range end; remember the half-open rule for ranges.
Key Takeaway

Use for to move through every element of a collection without manual index management.

Illustrative snippet
for letter in "Python":
    print(letter)

# Output:
# P
# y
# t
# h
# o
# n
Example explained: the loop variable letter takes each character, and the print function runs six times. This pattern is identical whether the sequence is a string or a list of objects.

screens.title: Iterating Over Strings
screens.narratorSegment: When you iterate over a string, each iteration gives you one character. This is useful for analysis tasks like counting vowels, removing punctuation, or transforming characters. For example, a vowel counter lowers the text then checks each character against the vowel set. The pattern is straightforward: the loop variable represents each character and a small conditional inside the loop updates a running count. A common pitfall is modifying the string while iterating; strings are immutable, so you should build a new result or collect characters into a list. Another misconception is counting only lowercase vowels; remembering to normalize the input to a single case avoids missed matches. Let's walk through a concrete program: first get the input and convert it to lowercase, initialize a counter to zero, then for each character check if it is in the string of vowels and increment the counter when true. At the end print the count. This example shows how for loops convert a potentially complex task into a small, clear structure. Try changing the vowel set or counting consonants to practice. Iterating Over Strings means each loop iteration provides one character, ideal for counting or transforming text with simple, clear logic.. In practical terms, character-by-character processing and a vowel counter example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Strings
Vowel counter — code
text = input("Enter a string: ").lower()
vowel_count = 0
for char in text:
    if char in "aeiou":
        vowel_count = vowel_count + 1
print(f"Number of vowels: {vowel_count}")
Explanation: lowercasing avoids case mismatches. The membership test uses the in operator, which reads clearly and avoids index arithmetic. The counter increments only when a vowel is found.
Notes and common mistakes
  • Do not modify the string while iterating. Build a new string or list instead.
  • Remember to normalize case to avoid missed matches.
  • Beware of accented vowels; this basic set counts only ASCII vowels.
Check your understanding

How would you change the code to count uppercase and accented vowels correctly?

screens.title: Using range() to Generate Sequences
screens.narratorSegment: The range function is a compact way to produce a sequence of integers for a for loop. The form range(n) yields values from zero up to n minus one. This half-open interval — including the start but excluding the stop — is intentional: range(n) always yields exactly n numbers, which matches a typical zero-based index pattern and avoids off-by-one mistakes. You can also call range with a start and stop to begin counting elsewhere, or with a start, stop, and step to skip values at a fixed stride. For example, range(2, 10) yields 2 through 9, and range(0, 10, 2) yields the even numbers 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Negative steps let you count backwards, such as range(10, 0, -1) to produce 10 down to 1. A common misunderstanding is expecting range to include the stop; always check the half-open behavior when translating math notation to code. Use range when you need a predictable count or when iterating over indexes. Try replacing a manual counter in a while loop with range to simplify code and reduce bugs. Using range() to Generate Sequences means range(start, stop, step) produces integers including start and excluding stop; it's ideal for counting loops and index-based iteration.. In practical terms, how range works and why it uses a half-open interval. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: range summary
keyIdea.text: range(start, stop, step) produces integers including start and excluding stop; it's ideal for counting loops and index-based iteration.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › range()
Common forms
for i in range(5):
    print(i)   # 0,1,2,3,4

for i in range(2, 10):
    print(i)   # 2..9

for i in range(0, 10, 2):
    print(i)   # 0,2,4,6,8

for i in range(10, 0, -1):
    print(i)   # 10 down to 1
Half-open intervals make counting and indexing consistent. If you need inclusive behavior, adjust the stop value accordingly.
Practical tips
  • Use range(len(sequence)) to iterate by index safely.
  • Pick a step when you want to skip items or generate even/odd numbers.
  • Use negative step to count backwards; ensure start and stop are set correctly.
Misconception

Expecting range to include the stop causes off-by-one errors. Check stop-1 when you need the final value.

screens.title: Start, Stop, Step — Variations of range()
screens.narratorSegment: The three-argument form of range — start, stop, step — lets you control the sequence precisely. The start value is the first number produced, stop is the end marker that is not produced, and step is the increment between successive numbers. For example, range(2, 10) produces integers from two to nine. When step is two, you skip every other number, which is perfect for listing even numbers. When step is negative, the sequence counts down; you must supply a start larger than stop for that to produce values. A frequent practical use is printing even numbers from 2 to 20 using range(2, 21, 2) — note the stop is 21 to include twenty because range excludes its stop. Another example is building countdown timers using a negative step. Pay attention to off-by-one issues: if you want to include the final value, set stop to final plus one when stepping positively. Small mistakes in the step or stop can silently produce empty sequences, so inspect the generated values when unsure. Start, Stop, Step — Variations of range() means range(start, stop, step) controls where counting begins, where it ends (excluded), and how it progresses between values.. In practical terms, how start and step change the produced sequence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Start/Step
keyIdea.text: range(start, stop, step) controls where counting begins, where it ends (excluded), and how it progresses between values.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Start / Step
Even numbers example
for i in range(2, 21, 2):
    print(i)   # 2,4,6,...,20
Note: stop is 21 to include 20. If you wrote range(2,20,2) you would stop at 18.
Countdown example
for i in range(10, 0, -1):
    print(i)   # 10,9,8,...,1
Be careful: if start <= stop and step is negative, the range is empty. Match step sign to start/stop direction.
Pro tip

When in doubt, print the list(range(...)) to inspect the generated numbers during development.

screens.title: Iterating Over Lists and enumerate()
screens.narratorSegment: Lists are one of the most common sequences to iterate. A basic for loop gives you each element in turn, which is ideal for processing or printing items. Sometimes you need both the item and its position. While you could use a separate index counter, Python's enumerate returns pairs of index and value so your loop cleanly receives both. For example, enumerating a list of fruits yields tuples containing the index and the fruit name; you can unpack them in the loop header into index and value variables. This reduces the chance of desynchronizing a separate counter and makes code clearer. A concrete example is printing '0: apple' and so on, which the enumerate pattern does directly. A common misconception is thinking enumerate always starts at one; by default it starts at zero to align with Python's zero-based indexing, but you can pass a different start value when needed. Use enumerate whenever index and item are both meaningful to the operation, such as ordered outputs, labeled reports, or when you need to update elements by index in a mutable sequence.

keyIdea.title: enumerate
keyIdea.text: Use enumerate(sequence) to get an index and value pair each iteration, avoiding manual counters.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Lists & enumerate()
List iteration
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

# Using enumerate:
for index, fruit in enumerate(fruits):
    print(f"{index}: {fruit}")
Enumerate returns tuples of (index, value). Unpack them directly in the for header for concise and readable code.
When to use enumerate
  • When output needs line numbers or labels.
  • When you need to update a list by index in place.
  • When pairing values with their position simplifies downstream logic.
Key Takeaway

Enumerate avoids manual index management and produces clearer, safer loops.

screens.title: zip() — Iterating in Parallel
screens.narratorSegment: zip lets you iterate over two or more sequences at the same time, producing tuples that pair elements from each sequence. It stops when the shortest sequence is exhausted, which is practical when you only have meaningful pairs up to that length. A common usage is matching names with ages, where you want to print 'Alice is 25 years old' by pairing the two lists. The main misuse is assuming zip pads shorter sequences; it does not. If one sequence is longer, extra items are ignored. If you need to preserve all items, consider iterating the longer sequence by index or using functions designed to fill missing values. Example: for name, age in zip(names, ages): print a formatted sentence. This pattern simplifies parallel processing and reduces index arithmetic. Remember that zip returns tuples, so unpack them in the for header. For debugging, convert zip to a list to inspect pairs. Try combining three sequences to see how zip groups triple items and how shortest-length behavior still applies. zip() — Iterating in Parallel means zip(a, b) pairs elements from sequences; it iterates until the shortest sequence ends, producing tuples for unpacking.. In practical terms, combine related sequences and loop over pairs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: zip
keyIdea.text: zip(a, b) pairs elements from sequences; it iterates until the shortest sequence ends, producing tuples for unpacking.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › zip()
Parallel iteration example
names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"]
ages = [25, 30, 35]
for name, age in zip(names, ages):
    print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
Zip pairs elements positionally. If ages had only two entries, Charlie would be ignored because zip stops with the shortest list.
When zip is not right
  • If you must keep all items from the longest list, zip will drop extras.
  • To pair by a matching key rather than position, use dictionaries or mapping logic.
Check

If lists differ in length, what happens to the extra items? Try it and inspect list(zip(...)).

screens.title: break and continue
screens.narratorSegment: break and continue let you change the normal sequential flow of a for loop. continue skips the remainder of the current iteration and proceeds to the next item, which is useful for filtering out unwanted cases early. break exits the loop entirely, often used when a search finds its match and there's no need to keep checking. For example, consider iterating numbers and skipping multiples of three with continue; when a number exceeds ten, break stops the loop. These controls are powerful but can make loops harder to follow if overused. A typical misuse is sprinkling many breaks and continues across nested loops without clear comments, which reduces readability. Use them judiciously: prefer clear loop conditions and well-named helper functions so the loop body remains simple. A concrete example is scanning for the first prime factor; break lets you stop once a factor is found. Always test edge cases where break might prevent finalization logic from running — sometimes a for-else clause can express 'didn't find a match' more clearly than a break flag. break and continue means use continue to skip the rest of the current iteration and break to stop the loop early when a goal is reached.. In practical terms, altering loop execution and common patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: break and continue let you change the normal sequential flow of a for loop. continue skips the remainder of the current iteration and proceeds to the next item, which is useful for filtering out unwanted cases early. break exits the loop entirely, often used when a search finds its match and there's no need to keep checking. For example, consider iterating numbers and skipping multiples of three with continue; when a number exceeds ten, break stops the loop. These controls are powerful but can make loops harder to follow if overused. A typical misuse is sprinkling many breaks and continues across nested loops without clear comments, which reduces readability. Use them judiciously: prefer clear loop conditions and well-named helper functions so the loop body remains simple. A concrete example is scanning for the first prime factor; break lets you stop once a factor is found. Always test edge cases where break might prevent finalization logic from running — sometimes a for-else clause can express 'didn't find a match' more clearly than a break flag. break and continue means use continue to skip the rest of the current iteration and break to stop the loop early when a goal is reached.. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › break & continue
Example: skip multiples of 3, stop after 10
for number in range(1, 20):
    if number % 3 == 0:
        continue  # Skip multiples of 3
    if number > 10:
        break     # Stop after 10
    print(number)

# Output: 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10
Use continue to filter and break to end early when you've achieved the loop's purpose.
Readability advice
  • Keep loop bodies short; extract helpers for complex conditions.
  • Prefer for-else when you want to detect a normal completion versus an early break.
Gotcha

break prevents a for-else else block from running; use this intentionally to detect whether a search found a match.

screens.title: for-else and Prime Detection
screens.narratorSegment: The for-else construct runs the else block only when the loop finishes without encountering a break. It's useful when you want to confirm that a search or test found nothing. A classic example finds prime numbers: for each candidate number, try dividing by possible factors; if a divisor is found, break and report the composite; if the inner loop completes with no break, the candidate is prime and the else clause runs. This pattern places the success action in the else block and the failure action alongside the break, making intent explicit. A common confusion is thinking the else belongs to the if; it belongs to the for and is conditional on normal completion. Use comments and clear variable names to avoid misreading this structure. For small ranges this pattern is readable and direct; for performance-critical prime testing, optimized algorithms are better, but the for-else example is pedagogically valuable because it shows how loop completion can be detected cleanly without flags. Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › for-else
Prime detection example
for n in range(2, 10):
    for x in range(2, n):
        if n % x == 0:
            print(f"{n} = {x} * {n//x}")
            break
    else:
        print(f"{n} is prime")
Here the else is paired with the inner for. It runs only when the inner loop did not hit break, indicating the number is prime.
Misreading caution

  • Use explicit comments when first learning for-else to clarify intent.
Check

Trace the code for n=4 and n=5. Which branch runs and why?

screens.title: for vs while
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing for versus while depends on whether you know the iteration count or whether repetition depends on a changing condition. Use for when you will visit each item in a known sequence, or when you know exactly how many iterations you need, such as counting from one to one hundred. For loops reduce the chance of mismanaging a loop variable because the sequence provides each step. Use while when you don't know how many times to repeat and the loop must continue until a condition changes, for example when repeatedly prompting a user until valid input is received or when waiting for a computation to converge. A frequent sign that a while loop could be rewritten as a for is an explicit counter that you increment each iteration; in that case range often makes the loop clearer and safer. Another common mistake is forgetting to update the while condition inside the loop, which can cause infinite loops. Compare examples to see the readability difference and prefer the construct that expresses the intent directly: counting and stepping use for; condition-driven repetition uses while.

keyIdea.title: When to use which loop
keyIdea.text: Use for for known counts and sequences; use while for condition-driven repetition when the iteration count is unknown.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › for vs while
For example — counting to 5
# Using for:
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)

# Using while:
i = 1
while i <= 5:
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
The for version is shorter and avoids the manual increment. If you find yourself writing the while version with a counter, prefer the for version with range.
When while is better
  • When repetition depends on user input or external conditions.
  • When stopping depends on a convergence threshold or signal arrival.
Misconception

Avoid converting a condition-driven loop into a for with an arbitrary large range; it may hide infinite loop logic and false assumptions.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll meet the for loop, the Python construct for visiting each element in a sequence. You'll learn why iteration is a core programming pattern, how range generates number sequences, and how helpers like enumerate and zip make indexed and parallel loops simple. We will also compare for to while so you know when each is better, and explore control tools such as break, continue, and the less obvious for-else. Practical examples include iterating through a string to inspect characters, using range to count, enumerating a list to obtain indexes and values together, and zipping two lists to step through related data in parallel. By the end you will be confident choosing a for loop when the number of steps is known or when processing every element in a collection is the goal. A short coding activity will help you apply these ideas: printing even numbers, a multiplication table, counting vowels, and drawing a triangle with asterisks. Notice how iteration moves work from manual counters to clear, less error-prone code. Ready to explore how a small loop can repeatedly do useful work? Let's begin.

By the end of these two objective screens you will be ready to write for loops that visit strings, ranges, and lists; use range to generate numeric sequences; choose for versus while with confidence; and iterate cleanly using the in operator. Each objective below is paired with a short explanation and a small visual cue so you can remember not just the what but the why. For loops are practical tools for processing each element in a collection; knowing the shape of the data tells you which helper to use. For example, range is ideal when counting from zero to n minus one, while enumerate pairs an index with each item when you need both. Using the in operator reads like plain language and prevents off-by-one errors. These objectives prepare you to write concise loops for tasks like printing sequences, counting matches, and combining parallel lists. Work toward the verified competency milestone by building the four small programs included in the hands-on activity. As you practice, notice when a while loop would be harder to read than a for loop.

These objectives focus on practice tasks and the utility functions you'll use while you practice. You'll apply range to count with predictable results, use enumerate when an index is required alongside a value, and apply zip when combining parallel lists such as names and ages. The hands-on activities in this chapter are specifically designed to reinforce these skills: printing even numbers exercises step and start values, the multiplication table practices range for a fixed count, the vowel counter shows iterating characters in a string, and the triangle program uses nested iteration patterns in a simple visual output. As you practice, watch for a common misconception: thinking range includes its end value. Remember that range uses a half-open interval which excludes the stop value; this choice prevents off-by-one errors and makes indexing align naturally with sequence lengths. After you complete the exercises, review your code to replace any manual counter-based while loops with for range loops where appropriate.

A for loop is a control structure that visits each element in a sequence and executes the loop body for that element. Think of iteration as walking along a list of items and performing the same action at each step. The loop variable takes on each value in the sequence in order, so you do not need to manage a manual counter unless you explicitly want an index. A concrete example is iterating over the string 'Python' where the loop variable becomes 'P', then 'y', and so on, and the print function outputs each character. A helpful analogy is a conveyor belt: items come past a single processing station and are transformed or inspected one at a time. This contrasts with a while loop, which keeps running as long as a condition is true and is better when you cannot predict the number of iterations up front. A common misconception is thinking for loops only work with numbers; in reality any iterable sequence — strings, lists, ranges — works. Key takeaway: use for when you have a collection to step through. A quick self-check: can you explain why a manual index is unnecessary when the sequence provides each element?

When you iterate over a string, each iteration gives you one character. This is useful for analysis tasks like counting vowels, removing punctuation, or transforming characters. For example, a vowel counter lowers the text then checks each character against the vowel set. The pattern is straightforward: the loop variable represents each character and a small conditional inside the loop updates a running count. A common pitfall is modifying the string while iterating; strings are immutable, so you should build a new result or collect characters into a list. Another misconception is counting only lowercase vowels; remembering to normalize the input to a single case avoids missed matches. Let's walk through a concrete program: first get the input and convert it to lowercase, initialize a counter to zero, then for each character check if it is in the string of vowels and increment the counter when true. At the end print the count. This example shows how for loops convert a potentially complex task into a small, clear structure. Try changing the vowel set or counting consonants to practice. In practical terms, character-by-character processing and a vowel counter example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The range function is a compact way to produce a sequence of integers for a for loop. The form range(n) yields values from zero up to n minus one. This half-open interval — including the start but excluding the stop — is intentional: range(n) always yields exactly n numbers, which matches a typical zero-based index pattern and avoids off-by-one mistakes. You can also call range with a start and stop to begin counting elsewhere, or with a start, stop, and step to skip values at a fixed stride. The three-argument form of range — start, stop, step — lets you control the sequence precisely. Lists are one of the most common sequences to iterate. A basic for loop gives you each element in turn, which is ideal for processing or printing items. These key concepts summarize the for loop essentials. First, a for loop iterates over each element in a sequence, such as strings, lists, and ranges. Second, range produces integer sequences using a half-open interval; remember that the stop value is excluded. Third, helpers like enumerate and zip make index-aware or parallel iteration concise and readable. Fourth, break and continue change loop flow: break exits early while continue skips the remainder of an iteration. Fifth, the for-else pattern runs the else block only when the loop completes without break, which is useful for search patterns.
